q: A team of four starts a new service on AWS. Nobody in the company runs Kubernetes today. Which platform is the usual default in 2026?
options: EKS with managed node groups, so the team can grow into Kubernetes later
ECS on Fargate, with one service per container image
Lambda for every route, behind API Gateway
EC2 virtual machines running PM2 in cluster mode
explain: ECS on Fargate runs containers without servers or a cluster to upgrade, which suits a small team with no Kubernetes skills. EKS is the right call when the company already operates Kubernetes and its ecosystem; adopting it "for later" means owning nodes, add-ons and upgrades now. Lambda fits scheduled or spiky work better than a whole service.

q: Why does the Dockerfile copy package.json and package-lock.json, run npm ci, and only then copy src?
options: So the install layer stays cached when only the source changes
Because npm ci refuses to run when source files are present
To make the final image smaller, since fewer files are copied into it
Because COPY src fails unless node_modules already exists in the stage
explain: Per Docker's cache docs, when a layer changes, every layer after it is rebuilt. Copying the manifests first means a commit that changes only src reuses the cached npm ci layer. The order does not change the size of the final image; the multi-stage build does that.

q: The build stage stays on node:24-trixie-slim, but someone switches only the runtime stage to node:24-alpine to save space. The service uses a native addon compiled during npm ci. What is the risk?
options: Alpine images cannot run as a non-root user, so the pod security context rejects them
There is no Node 24 image for Alpine, so the stage silently falls back to an older Node
Alpine uses musl, not glibc, so the addon built in the Debian stage may not load
Alpine images end up larger than slim ones once the addon's libraries are added
explain: The docker-node README states that Alpine uses musl libc and that programs built for Debian's glibc in general do not run on it. The addon was compiled against glibc in the build stage, so it can fail at runtime. Alpine is in fact about 25 % smaller than slim, which is why people try it; build and run on the same libc.

q: The Dockerfile ends with CMD node dist/server.js (shell form). What happens on docker stop?
options: Node receives SIGTERM directly and runs its graceful shutdown handler
Docker sends SIGINT for shell-form commands instead, and Node exits on SIGINT by default
The container restarts at once, because the shell exits with code 143
/bin/sh -c does not pass the signal, so the container is killed after 10 seconds
explain: Docker's reference says the shell form runs the command under /bin/sh -c, which does not pass signals, so the program does not receive SIGTERM from docker stop. After the 10-second default the daemon sends SIGKILL, and requests in flight are cut. The exec form ["node", "dist/server.js"] fixes it.

q: Why does the workflow reference actions/checkout@3d3c42e… instead of actions/checkout@v7?
options: A tag can be moved to other code; a full commit SHA cannot
GitHub runs SHA-pinned actions faster, because their code is cached on the runner image
Version tags are not allowed for actions published by GitHub
A SHA makes the action update itself to the latest release
explain: GitHub's security guide says a tag "can be moved or deleted" if someone gains access to the action's repository. That happened in March 2026, when 76 of the 77 tags of trivy-action were force-pushed to malicious code. A SHA pins the exact code; updates come from a bot such as Dependabot proposing a new SHA.

q: The ECR repository has tag immutability on. A script tries to push a hotfix build under the tag 3f9c2a1, which the current release already uses. What happens?
options: ECR moves the tag to the new image and keeps the old image untagged in the repository
ECR stores both images under the same tag
The push is rejected with ImageTagAlreadyExistsException
ECR accepts the push but blocks pulls of the new image
explain: Per the ECR docs, once tag immutability is on, pushing an image with a tag already in the repository returns ImageTagAlreadyExistsException. That guarantee is what makes "this tag means this commit" true. Overwriting the tag is what a mutable repository, the default, would do.

q: In the deploy role's trust policy, what does the condition sub = repo:shop/orders-api:environment:production achieve?
options: It gives the role access to the production AWS account
Only that repository's jobs targeting production can assume the role
It keeps the temporary credentials valid until the environment is deleted in GitHub
It encrypts the OIDC token with the environment's secrets
explain: The sub claim of GitHub's OIDC token names the repository and the context of the job; with an environment, it is repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME. Matching it with StringEquals means a pull request run (subject …:pull_request) or another repository cannot assume the role. The condition restricts who; the permissions policy decides what.

q: The Orders API pods use EKS Pod Identity. What must the application code do to get AWS credentials?
options: Call STS AssumeRole at startup with the role ARN, then refresh it every hour
Read the access key and secret from a Kubernetes Secret mounted into the pod
Pass the service account token to every client constructor
Nothing: clients created without credentials use the SDK's default chain
explain: Per the EKS docs, EKS sets environment variables in the pod's containers that point the AWS SDKs to the Pod Identity Agent, which issues temporary, rotated credentials. The default credential chain picks them up, so new S3Client({}) is enough. A static key in a Secret is exactly what Pod Identity removes.

q: With Helm 4, the deploy step runs helm upgrade --install orders-api ./chart with no wait or rollback option. The new pods crash-loop. What does the CI job report?
options: Success: without a wait option, Helm 4 waits only for hooks
Failure: Helm 4 always waits until every pod of the Deployment is ready
Failure, and Helm rolls back to the previous release automatically
The job hangs until the 5-minute default timeout, then fails
explain: Helm 4's upgrade docs give hookOnly as the wait strategy when --wait is omitted, so the command returns once the manifests are applied. Add --wait, or --rollback-on-failure, which also sets the wait to watcher and returns to the last successful release on failure.

q: The API never downloads exports itself, yet its IAM policy grants s3:GetObject on exports/*. Why?
options: S3 requires it on any request that lists or reads objects in the bucket
Without it, the API could not write new exports into the exports/ prefix
A presigned URL uses the signer's permissions, so the API needs them
It lets the API run the CSV generation inside S3 instead of in the pod
explain: Per the S3 docs, a presigned URL works only if it was created by a principal allowed to perform the operation it represents. The API signs download links, so its role needs s3:GetObject on those keys, and nothing broader. Listing a bucket needs s3:ListBucket, and writing needs s3:PutObject, which this role does not have.

q: Why does the export Lambda create its pg pool and its S3 client at the top level of the module, and give the pool max: 1?
options: Top-level code runs again before each invocation, which keeps the connection fresh
Init runs once per environment and is reused; an environment runs one invocation at a time
Lambda forbids opening network connections inside the handler function itself
max: 1 is required by RDS Proxy, which rejects any client pool holding more than one connection
explain: The Lambda docs recommend initialising SDK clients and database connections outside the handler, because the init phase runs once per environment and later invocations reuse them. Each environment serves one request at a time, so a second connection would sit idle and count against the database's limit. Top-level code does not run again for each invocation.

q: Two engineers start terraform apply on the same state at the same moment. The S3 backend has use_lockfile = true. What happens?
options: Both applies run, and the one that finishes last overwrites the state
Terraform merges both plans into one and applies them in order
S3 versioning rejects the second write of the state file
The second run fails to acquire the lock and stops
explain: Locking exists so that one run at a time can write a state. With use_lockfile, generally available since Terraform 1.11, the lock is a file stored next to the state in S3, and the second run fails to acquire it. Versioning only keeps old copies of the state; it does not prevent concurrent writes.

q: An interviewer asks: "Lambda or containers for the Orders API itself?" It serves a steady 400 requests per second all day, each about 80 ms and mostly waiting on PostgreSQL, with Black Friday peaks five times higher, and the company runs EKS. What is the best answer?
options: Lambda, because it scales to zero and is therefore the cheapest option at any traffic level
Lambda behind API Gateway, since cold starts no longer exist on the Node 24 runtime
Containers on the existing EKS cluster, with Lambda kept for side jobs like the export
One large EC2 instance, so that the whole API shares a single connection pool
explain: Steady traffic keeps containers busy, while Lambda would bill every environment for its full duration, database waits included, with one request per environment and one set of connections each. The company already runs EKS, so the marginal cost is low. Scaling to zero helps only workloads with idle time, and cold starts still exist.

q: In review you find this Dockerfile, and the repository has no .dockerignore. What do you ask to fix first?
code:
FROM node:24-trixie-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
options: Multi-stage, manifests before source, npm ci, and a .dockerignore
Switch CMD to the shell form so that environment variables are expanded at start
Move to node:24-alpine first, because the image size is the main risk here
Add EXPOSE 3000, otherwise Kubernetes cannot send traffic to the container
explain: COPY . . before the install rebuilds the dependencies on every commit and, without a .dockerignore, copies the host's node_modules and .env into an image the company can pull. A single stage also ships the compiler and dev dependencies, and npm install does not install the lockfile exactly. The shell form would break signal delivery; EXPOSE is documentation.

q: The image ends with USER node. The pod sets securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true and no runAsUser. What happens when the pod starts?
options: It starts normally, because the node user of the image is not root
It starts as root, because Kubernetes ignores the USER line of the image
Kubernetes replaces the user with uid 65534 (nobody) and starts it
It fails to start: the kubelet cannot verify a non-numeric user
explain: With runAsNonRoot and no runAsUser, the kubelet checks the image's user, and its source returns the error "image has non-numeric user (node), cannot verify user is non-root". Write USER 1000 in the Dockerfile or set runAsUser: 1000. Kubernetes uses the image's user when no runAsUser is set; it does not ignore it.

q: The build installs a private npm package, so a colleague adds ARG NPM_TOKEN and passes it with --build-arg. What do you suggest?
options: It is fine if the next RUN deletes the .npmrc that holds the token
Use a secret mount: build arguments persist in the image
Move the token to an ENV line, because ENV values are not stored in the image
Keep the build argument, but push the image only to a private registry
explain: Docker's documentation says build arguments and ENV values persist in the final image, and M12 treats such a token as leaked to everyone who can pull. A secret mount exposes the token as a file during one RUN without writing it to a layer. Deleting a file in a later layer leaves it in the earlier one, and a private registry does not make the token secret.

q: Two pull requests are merged one minute apart. The second merge cancels the first workflow run while its helm upgrade is halfway through. Which setting causes this, and what is the fix?
options: The group name: use github.sha instead, so that two runs never share a group
Nothing in this block: Helm cancels itself whenever a newer release starts
cancel-in-progress also cancels runs on main: limit it to pull requests
The workflow lacks permissions: actions: write, so GitHub cancels it
explain: GitHub documents that cancel-in-progress: true cancels the running job or workflow in the same group, and every push to main shares the refs/heads/main group. An expression such as github.event_name == 'pull_request' limits cancellation to pull requests, and a deploy-production group with cancel-in-progress: false serialises deploys. A per-SHA group would allow two deploys at once.

q: Production manifests use orders-api:latest, pushed by every merge to main. During an incident, what is the main problem?
options: Nobody knows which commit runs, and there is nothing precise to roll back to
ECR does not scan images whose only tag is latest, so CVEs go unnoticed
Kubernetes refuses to pull an image tagged latest in a production namespace
The latest tag makes every pull download the full image, which slows deploys
explain: A movable tag says nothing about content: a pod rescheduled after a new push can pull a newer image than its neighbours, and "roll back to latest" means nothing. Commit-SHA tags in an immutable repository, deployed by digest, fix all three. ECR scans by image, not by tag name, and Kubernetes pulls latest without complaint.

q: This condition is in the trust policy of orders-api-deploy. What is the risk?
options: None: the audience check already limits the role to the Orders API workflows
Only forks of shop/orders-api in other organisations can now assume the role
The credentials now last 12 hours instead of the default of one hour
Any repository, branch or pull request of the shop organisation can deploy
explain: The wildcard matches every subject that starts with repo:shop/, so every repository, branch and pull request of the organisation qualifies. The audience only proves the token was minted for STS, by any GitHub workflow. Pin the subject with StringEquals to repo:shop/orders-api:environment:production. Session duration is set by the role and the action, not by this condition.

q: Pod Identity is configured for the Orders API, yet CloudTrail shows its S3 calls signed by the IAM user vm-legacy. What is the most likely cause?
options: Pod Identity falls back to IAM users whenever the node agent is overloaded
An old AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in the pod wins: the SDK checks env vars first
CloudTrail logs Pod Identity calls under the last IAM user that edited the role
The bucket policy forces every request to be signed by that IAM user
explain: The SDK for JavaScript v3 tries fromEnv() before the container credential provider, so leftover static keys silently win. Remove the variables from the pod, then deactivate the key in IAM. CloudTrail records the identity that really signed the request, which is why it reveals the problem.

q: The nightly drift job runs terraform plan -detailed-exitcode on production and exits with code 2. What does it mean, and what do you do?
options: Terraform crashed during the refresh; rerunning the job usually clears it
The state is locked by another run; delete the lock file and rerun
Changes are present: inspect them, then codify or revert
No changes: exit code 2 only means that two providers were checked
explain: Per the plan docs, exit code 0 is an empty diff, 1 an error, and 2 a successful plan with changes. A refresh-only plan shows what changed outside Terraform; the team then writes the change into the code or applies to undo it, after reading the plan. Never auto-apply a drift fix: the console change may have been an incident fix.

q: Version 42 renamed orders.total to orders.total_cents in the same migration and is broken. The team rolls back to the digest of version 41. What happens?
options: Version 41 fails on queries that read orders.total
The rollback also reverts the migration, so version 41 works again
Helm detects the schema change and refuses to roll the release back
Kubernetes keeps the version 42 pods running until the migration is undone
explain: Redeploying a digest changes the code, never the database. A rename in one step breaks the previous version, which is why migrations follow expand and contract (M10): add the new column, write both, switch reads, and drop the old one only when no running version needs it. Neither Helm nor Kubernetes knows anything about the schema.

q: The repository is private, the company is on GitHub Team, and the production environment lists two required reviewers. Deploys still run without any approval. Why?
options: Required reviewers only apply to jobs that read secrets from the environment
The deploy job also needs permissions: deployments: write to request approval
Approvals given on earlier runs carry over to the following runs
On Free, Pro and Team, required reviewers work only in public repositories
explain: GitHub's environments documentation states that on the Free, Pro and Team plans, required reviewers and wait timers are only available for public repositories. A private repository needs a higher plan for this gate, or another one, such as a protected branch that only release managers can push to. Approvals are per run; they do not carry over.

q: The export Lambda used to e-mail a presigned link created with expiresIn of seven days. Customers report that links fail after a few hours. Why, and what is the fix?
options: S3 caps presigned URLs at one hour, so the e-mail must be resent every hour
It expired with the role's temporary credentials; sign at click time
A bucket lifecycle rule deleted the files; lifecycle rules must be disabled
Seven days exceeds the SDK maximum, so it silently signs for one hour
explain: Per the S3 docs, a URL signed with temporary credentials expires when those credentials do, even if it asked for longer; seven days is only possible with long-term IAM user credentials, which the team just removed. Signing at click time in GET /exports/orders.csv keeps links short-lived and needs no long-term key. The CLI and SDKs accept up to seven days.

q: EventBridge Scheduler retried the nightly export after a timeout, and finance found two files for the same night: orders-2026-10-29-a81f.csv and orders-2026-10-29-c3d0.csv. Which change makes retries safe?
options: Turn off retries on the schedule, so each night runs exactly once
Add a random delay before the export so two attempts never overlap
Derive the key from the scheduled time, so a retry overwrites
Raise the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes so the export never times out
explain: Scheduler delivers at least once, so the handler must be idempotent; the scheduled time is the same for every attempt of a run, so a key derived from it turns a retry into an overwrite. Turning retries off trades duplicates for missing exports, and a longer timeout reduces retries without removing them.

q: The team considers moving the payment webhook to Lambda. On Black Friday it receives 2,000 calls per second, each taking 0.5 s. What happens with default settings?
options: 1,000 environments: the whole default regional quota, and 1,000 connections
4,000 environments, and Lambda queues the extra calls until one is free
A single environment, because Node handles all those concurrent calls asynchronously
2,000 environments, one for each call arriving in the same second
explain: Concurrency = 2,000 requests per second × 0.5 s = 1,000, which equals the default per-region concurrency quota, so the other functions of the account get throttled too. Each environment handles one request at a time and opens its own connections, ten times PostgreSQL's default limit of 100, so this design also needs RDS Proxy and reserved concurrency.

q: After moving aws_db_instance.orders into modules/postgres, the plan shows the old address "will be destroyed" and module.orders_db.aws_db_instance.this "will be created". What is the right fix?
options: Apply, then restore the database from the final snapshot
Run terraform apply -refresh-only so Terraform notices the move
Add create_before_destroy so the new database exists before the old one goes
Add a moved block from the old address to the new one
explain: Terraform tracks objects by address, so a new address looks like a new resource and the missing one like a deletion. A moved block renames the address in the state without touching the object. create_before_destroy would create a second, empty database; restoring from a snapshot loses every order written since.

q: A "cleanup" pull request deletes the whole module "orders_db" call. Inside the module, the RDS resource has lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }. What actually stops the database from being deleted?
options: prevent_destroy, which stays recorded in the state after the block is removed
deletion_protection, which AWS enforces whatever the tool
Nothing: once merged, the apply deletes the database whatever is set
The S3 backend, which refuses plans that remove whole modules
explain: The lifecycle docs say prevent_destroy does not prevent destruction once the resource's configuration is removed, because the setting disappears with the block. deletion_protection is an attribute of the AWS instance, so RDS refuses the delete call. A plan guard on protected types and a final snapshot add two more layers.

q: The guard script of section 11 runs on this plan.json. What does it print, and with which exit code?
options: "No protected resource is deleted." with exit code 0, because the database is recreated first
Both addresses, because both plans contain a delete
It flags module.orders_db.aws_db_instance.this (create, delete) and exits with code 1
It throws, because ["create", "delete"] is not a valid action list
explain: A replacement is written as two actions, and includes('delete') catches both orders, as Terraform's JSON format docs intend; create-before-destroy still destroys the old database. The SQS queue is not a protected type, so only the database is listed. Measured on Node 24.11 with this exact plan: one line, exit code 1.

q: "How do you ship a Node service to production?" Which answer would convince a senior interviewer?
options: PR checks, one scanned SHA-tagged image, an approved OIDC deploy by digest that rolls back, reviewed Terraform
We build the image on each server with docker compose up --build, which keeps staging and production identical
GitHub Actions with an administrator access key in the repository secrets, deploying latest on every push
We use Kubernetes, so the platform itself takes care of shipping, health checks and rollback
explain: The first answer follows one commit and names the risk each step removes: untested code, unknown images, long-lived keys, unready pods, unreviewed infrastructure. Building on the server recreates the VM problem, an admin key and latest are what this module removes, and "Kubernetes takes care of it" names a tool without a process.
